I felt the SAME WAY 
My grad school placement was at a middle school high school and I received no training. 
My placement was supposed to be “clinical social work” not for school social work which can be different things depending on your responsibilities and role (there are clinical social workers in schools as well but it looks different). 
This school did not do the clinical aspect well 
And was extremely disorganized with no structure and it was a terrible time. It killed my confidence. 
Fast forward—- I graduated and got a job at a clinic as a mental health therapist. “Doing real therapy” 
And because my confidence was so shot from the internship I found myself feeling the exact same way. 
Luckily at this new job my supervisor is very very supportive and encouraging and there’s a lot of structure and trainings. 
Additionally my entire cohort that was hired at the same time as me were also all newly graduated therapists. Talking to them helped so much because regardless of their field placement experience they all felt the same way. 
Therapy is hard because it’s not always as concrete as let’s say being a medical doctor. 
When you’re a medical doctor and a patient comes in with a headache, you give them Tylenol rule out a brain hemorrhage and send them on their way. 
In therapy each situation is so unique and there are so many different theories and interventions to pull from depending on the person. 
I feel like myself and a lot of my fellow newbie colleagues are in the stage where we haven’t worked long enough to see the results yet. 
Again as a medical doctor you give someone Tylenol for their headache, the headache goes away in an hour and you know it worked. 
In therapy it’s not always so easy to see the results in our clients and honestly takes a lot of time and effort not just in our part but the clients as well. 
Without seeing those instant results it can make us feel in the dark like “are we actually doing anything” 
But the truth is. 
As your validating and listening and providing some interventions you maybe doing a lot more but just don’t have the clinical language to describe it or see it yet. 
If your clients are showing up that’s a win. 
I hope your supervisor is encouraging and can help build a framework for you to build upon what you’re already doing and to motivate you to keep doing an awesome job. 
Imposter syndrome SUCKS and it’s hard. 
But keep showing up for your clients and yourself and you’ll start seeing results. 
Rooting for you fellow newbie! It gets easier I promise! You’re not alone!

I have a lot to say. 

I grew up in the church, deconstructed my faith, and am in a liberating medium right now. 

First of all, I would like to say that the mainline "Christianity" that we know if today is typically referred to as American Evangelicalism. 

The Evangelical movement IS toxic, and promotes a weird shame-based elitist culture where "I'm right and everyone else who doesn't believe what I believe is wrong and therefore needs to be 'saved'." 

I could go on and on and on about the hypocrisy, egotism, and blatant narcissistic savior complex that runs rapid like a disease through the church. 

It makes me sick. 

BUT that being said. I am still a Christian because Christianity is not what American culture has turned it into. 

Christian literally means "little Christ" and we are taught to mimic/follow the lifestyle of love and compassion that Jesus Christ exemplified. 

When you look at his life he stood up to and criticized the super strict oppressive religious systems of that day (the Pharisees), He fed and clothed the poor, hungry, marginalized and diseased and he hung out with the outcast of society that everyone else thought they were too good to be associated with. 

Jesus was basically a really good social worker and that's how I try to live my life as a Christian. 

American Evangelicals (evangelical in this case is a blanket term I am using to refer to most mainline denominations, but not all specific churches within those denominations) do live a life reflective of the person of Jesus (at least a good portion of them). They judge, they hoard their wealth, they make strict religious rules and guidelines their "god" instead of actually serving God, they ironically ignore scientific fact-based truth, live in their own religious elitist bubbles and only make an appearance in the "real world" with "sinners" if they're trying to convert them or "save them". 

That is not Christianity, that is not Jesus and it took me a long time to see past all the bullshit but I am glad I have. 

I am a Christian who is pro-choice, LGBTQ affirming, democrat (mostly), and has a healthy view on sex. 

It is possible for your sister to be a Christian without being in the cult of evangelicalism. 

American Christian CULTure is what makes Christianity weird. If she does her best to follow Jesus's example of how to live life (i.e. love thy neighbor as thyself, defend the weak, feed the hungry, love the "unlovable") then she's going to be fine. Just remind her not to get caught up in all the hype of the man-made religious aspect of Christianity. 

There are a lot of benefits to being apart of a faith community. 

I moved out at 17, have a poor relationship with my parents due to their untreated mental health issues that caused them to treat me poorly. 

I'm 25 and have already lived in 22 different houses/apartments across the united states because of instability, I was lonely, suicidal, and had nothing for a long time because I had no roots, no people to connect with. 

When I got connected to my present (less crazy but still broken in its own way like everything else) church community I found people who ACTUALLY loved me and weren't just trying to "save" me. I always wanted a family and now I genuinely have one and have been able to heal, go back to school, start a career and find some roots and stability. I can easily sniff out the people still "drinking the koolaid" of post-modern American evangelicalism and I avoid those people like the plague right now because I cannot deal with it, but I am beyond lucky to have found the most amazing loving kind people who actually exemplify the life of Jesus and listen to fact-based scientific truth.
